Scientists are reconstructing the Bantu expansion, a migration from western Africa starting 6,000 to 4,000 years ago that introduced farming and metalworking to sub-Saharan Africa.
Daily News

Science · Geography

The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.

Africa · Notable · New

Briefing produced 08 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Scientists are reconstructing the Bantu expansion, a migration from western Africa starting 6,000 to 4,000 years ago that introduced farming and metalworking to sub-Saharan Africa. A 2024 genomic analysis of 1,763 Africans found the greatest genetic diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa, supporting a population expansion from that region. Archaeological evidence, including pottery in the Congo rainforest dating to 2,300–2,000 years ago, suggests Bantu groups crossed the forest together before splitting into east- and south-moving groups 2,500 to 3,500 years ago.

Why it matters

The expansion reshaped sub-Saharan Africa's demography, introducing sedentary lifestyles and metalworking to hunter-gatherer regions. Today, approximately 350 million Africans speak Bantu languages, and many carry Bantu ancestry, making this one of history's largest human migrations.

Conflict · Politics · Economy

US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections

Global · Iran · United States · Major · Previously featured

Briefing produced 08 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

US officials stated that the US carried out limited, defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps firing on a US aircraft. The strikes occurred on Monday, just before US midterm elections, while mediators from Qatar and Pakistan facilitated negotiations to prevent a return to all-out war. Iranian negotiators had previously proposed reopening the strait within two days if the US met seven conditions, including lifting a naval blockade and releasing frozen assets.

Why it matters

The Strait of Hormuz is a critical global energy chokepoint through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass. Its effective closure due to the conflict and US naval blockade has disrupted commercial shipping, prompting US military protection for tankers and intense diplomatic efforts to restore stability.

More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak

DR Congo · Kenya · Nigeria · Uganda · Major · Previously featured

More than 5,000 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo's ongoing Ebola outbreak, which began in May and is now the country's deadliest in history. The epidemic has affected eight provinces, with over 10,300 confirmed cases and a 48.6% case fatality rate. The Ituri province remains the epicentre, while cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda. No vaccine exists for the Bundibugyo strain, though clinical trials are underway.

Why it matters

The outbreak is spreading rapidly in a conflict zone, complicating containment efforts. Health workers have faced violent attacks, and the UN warns the current outbreak is taking lives at a much faster rate than previous incidents.

Software squeezes more data out of Webb Telescope for imaging exoplanets

Global · Notable · Catch up

Briefing produced 08 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Researchers developed FLIP, a software package that uses gradient descent to optimize a physical model of the James Webb Space Telescope's NIRCam hardware. By tuning 10^6 parameters, FLIP reduces noise in exoplanet imaging, boosting signal-to-noise ratios by 1.5 to 2 times in tests. The method enabled the first detection of a planet at a carbon dioxide wavelength and increased sensitivity by a factor of 15 for the specific star TYC 5899.

Why it matters

FLIP lowers observational noise, enabling the potential detection of dimmer, older, or lower-mass exoplanets that were previously undetectable. Researchers also propose modifying the tool to provide insights into telescope hardware behavior.

Science · Geography

Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity

Global · Notable · Updated

Briefing produced 08 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

A study in Nature proposes that slow mantle convection pushed the ancient continent of Laurentia up for hundreds of millions of years, creating a surface that glaciers then eroded to form the Great Unconformity. The researchers argue that this combination of gentle uplift and glacial scouring explains why the geological gap is prominent in North America but less distinct elsewhere, though they note that mantle dynamics were likely one of several contributing factors to the subsequent Cambrian explosion.

Why it matters

The findings suggest that deep Earth processes may have influenced the timing of the Cambrian explosion by washing eroded rock material into the oceans, potentially fertilizing them with calcium just before life began forming shells and skeletons.

Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights

Global · Notable · Catch up

Briefing produced 08 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Arizona State University researchers identified an epigenetic mechanism explaining why large dogs age faster than small ones, finding that giant breeds lose roughly 35 percent more LINE1 DNA methylation annually than small breeds. This reduced regulation of "jumping genes" is linked to increased DNA damage and age-related diseases. The study, published in Science, used data from 864 dogs to map these methylation patterns across the genome.

Why it matters

The findings provide a clear molecular signature for the size-lifespan trade-off in dogs, offering a valuable model for biologists to study aging mechanisms in other mammals.

A study in Nature proposes that slow mantle convection pushed the ancient continent of Laurentia up for hundreds of millions of years, creating a surface that glaciers then eroded to form the Great Unconformity. The researchers argue that this combination of gentle uplift and glacial scouring explains why the geological gap is prominent in North America but less distinct elsewhere, though they note that mantle dynamics were likely one of several contributing factors to the subsequent Cambrian explosion.

Why it matters

The findings suggest that deep Earth processes may have influenced the timing of the Cambrian explosion by washing eroded rock material into the oceans, potentially fertilizing them with calcium just before life began forming shells and skeletons.

Extending Hubble's life would preserve unique visible and ultraviolet observation capabilities that current successor telescopes do not fully replace, with the next comparable observatory not expected until the 2040s.

The features address privacy concerns by using on-device processing and Apple’s Private Cloud Compute, ensuring raw audio is not accessible to Apple and recaps are deleted from servers immediately after generation.
